principles.title: The model is one component
principles.text: The model predicts a response from the request it receives. Nova's surrounding software chooses context, invokes capabilities, stores results and decides when another model request is needed.

principles.title: Most arrows are not network links
principles.text: Python imports, function calls, callbacks and queues can all stay inside one process. HTTP and WebSocket arrows cross a transport boundary. Use the connection type before thinking in ports or packets.

principles.title: State and knowledge are different
principles.text: A task status is structured state. A journal is readable history. A vector index is a way to find related material. A prompt is the selected information the model sees for this request.

principles.title: A feature needs a complete path
principles.text: A file can exist and pass its own checks while no normal request reaches it. Trace the trigger, caller, payload, execution, result and consumer before concluding that a capability is integrated.

boundary_boot.why: A set of Python files and model weights does nothing until processes start in the right order and share the intended runtime.
boundary_boot.analogy: Service startup and dependency ordering: a listener being open is only one readiness signal.
inputs: Model paths, ports and boot configuration
outputs: A shared runtime attached to the chat app
boundary_boot.failure: A port may be occupied by old code, or a flag may be omitted even while the UI opens normally.
change: Check which launcher the user actually invokes.
Trace configuration into the final process arguments.
Verify the loaded process separately from the files on disk.

boundary_chat.why: The conversation interface translates human activity into the context and callbacks consumed by the body.
boundary_chat.analogy: An application gateway that also assembles the request body; removing it can change more than presentation.
inputs: Session history, written context and relevant archive snippets
outputs: Streamed output, persisted messages and memory ingestion requests
boundary_chat.failure: The model can answer coherently from incomplete context if the latest message or identity files never reach the request.
change: Inspect context assembly before changing prompts.
Preserve the callback signatures used by the runtime.
Check a normal reply and an autonomous wake as separate paths.

nova_runtime.why: Nova needs a coordinator that owns her lifecycle and wake cycle independently of one particular communication interface.
nova_runtime.analogy: A service supervisor plus an event loop. It coordinates work; it is not the language model itself.
inputs: Perception, busy state, tasks and model availability
outputs: Events, model calls and background-worker lifecycle
nova_runtime.failure: The UI can be alive while autonomy never reaches an executable action phase, or a headless run can have less context than chat.
change: Trace the relevant boot mode and shared-runtime instance.
Identify whether the host supplies a callback or the body supplies a default.
Check busy-state release, interruption and result persistence as well as generation.

nova_cortex.why: The body needs explicit policies and state for deciding what to do, tracking work and checking claims against evidence.
nova_cortex.analogy: Application control logic and policy decisions, with receipts as the audit trail.
outputs: Witness verdicts, verification requests and specialist choices
nova_cortex.failure: A plausible decision or verdict may be detached from actual observations. An old task can persist without being advanced.
change: Find the state or evidence the decision actually reads.
Keep a proposed action distinct from a performed action.
Check both accepted and rejected decisions, including missing evidence.

nova_voice.why: Model output needs a controlled loop that can distinguish thoughts, replies and requested actions, then feed real results back into reasoning.
nova_voice.analogy: A protocol interpreter and transaction loop around an inference service.
inputs: Model token streams and action results
nova_voice.failure: A tool request may appear in a channel the parser ignores, or a drafted claim may reach the user without the result it depends on.
change: Trace reasoning_content and content separately.
Follow requested action → dispatcher → result → next model request.
Keep the final reply boundary and failure/timeout paths visible.

nova_senses.why: Reasoning about the machine or surroundings needs observations supplied by code, not plausible text invented by the model.
nova_senses.analogy: Sensors and telemetry collectors: source, freshness and target matter as much as the value.
inputs: Time, hardware, environment and interaction signals
Host images, windows or requested web material
outputs: Observations and descriptions for context or tools
nova_senses.failure: Nova can describe the wrong display, stale activity or an unavailable sensor as if it were current unless the result carries that distinction.
change: Identify the exact host/display/input being observed.
Trace how the observation reaches the prompt or action result.
Check unavailable and stale inputs without substituting plausible data.

nova_lancedb.why: The model's current request cannot contain every prior interaction, so code needs a bounded way to retrieve potentially relevant material.
nova_lancedb.analogy: A search index over stored records. Similarity ranking is a retrieval mechanism, not a truth check.
inputs: A query to embed and compare
outputs: A bounded archive excerpt for context or an explicit recall action
nova_lancedb.failure: Saving, indexing, matching and injecting are separate steps. A record on disk may never appear in the next model request.
change: Trace the write path and read path independently.
Check embedding model, vector dimensions and retrieval limits together.
Verify the retrieved text is actually inserted into the intended request.

nova_logs.why: You need durable records to distinguish what Nova attempted, performed and merely said.
nova_logs.analogy: Logging and retention infrastructure. Missing telemetry is not proof that an event did or did not happen.
nova_logs.failure: A live UI event may vanish without a durable receipt, or a dedicated writer may bypass a shared logger.
change: Identify the actual writer for the record you need.
Keep event names, timestamps and request/turn identifiers consistent.
Check failures in the logging path itself.

nova_imagination.why: Image creation requires a workflow, model assets and an external generation service; a language-model request alone does not render an image.
nova_imagination.analogy: A job client that submits work to another service and collects its artifact.
outputs: Returned image paths or failure information
nova_imagination.failure: Submission can succeed while polling, asset selection or output collection fails.
change: Follow request construction, submission, polling and retrieval.
Check the actual asset names and service endpoint.
Treat a submitted job separately from a usable returned image.

nova_forge.why: Created capabilities need a discoverable interface and a dispatch path before the rest of Nova can use them.
nova_forge.analogy: A plugin loader and registry with a contract for discovery and invocation.
inputs: Capability names, designs and created files
nova_forge.failure: A created file may exist without being discoverable, or a dynamically loaded function can violate the expected contract.
change: Inspect the loader and the interface it expects.
Check missing, malformed and failing capabilities.
Keep detachable implementation details outside body coupling.

nova_play.why: Curiosity needs a concrete way to obtain material and retain selected results, beyond a prompt asking the model to be curious.
nova_play.analogy: An optional content acquisition path and a small saved collection.
nova_play.failure: Network failure or malformed content can leave the exploration request with no usable material.
change: Trace acquisition separately from saving.
Keep external text as input data rather than execution authority.
Check unavailable sources and empty results.

nova_computer.why: A computer faculty needs a stable contract for shell and GUI actions across available backends.
nova_computer.analogy: An abstraction over execution environments. Backend availability and end-to-end command routing are separate checks.
outputs: Command results, screenshots and backend status
nova_computer.failure: Standalone Hands can work while no ordinary conversation request reaches it. Host screenshots and the separate desktop can also be confused.
change: Start at the caller and prove it reaches the backend.
Identify the X display and shell used for both action and observation.
Check result/receipt delivery before calling the feature integrated.

nova_memory.why: These older helpers express journaling, goals and state operations, but the current main paths can write those files elsewhere.
nova_memory.analogy: A legacy abstraction alongside direct storage access. Similar names do not prove a shared path.
inputs: Helper calls, proposed goals or state preconditions
nova_memory.failure: Assuming all memory flows through this package leads to fixes in code that the normal path never calls.
change: Inspect inbound callers before extending a helper.
Compare direct writes in tool_router with this package.
Check whether the old retirement plan changed; do not remove code from an import count alone.

nova_config.why: A settings helper centralizes defaults only when the real call paths consume it.
nova_config.analogy: A configuration source with a possible split-brain problem if other modules read their own defaults.
outputs: Settings values for callers that use this helper
nova_config.failure: Editing one settings file can have no effect if the executing module uses an environment variable or another literal instead.
change: Trace a setting from its definition to the actual consumer.
Check precedence between files, environment and runtime values.
Use an observable consumer-side check after changing a default.

nova_witness.why: Changing an evidence-checking model needs repeatable cases and a way to compare errors and latency.
nova_witness.analogy: An evaluation harness: recorded inputs, expected outcomes and repeatable test runs.
nova_witness.failure: A separate model may be running but have worse judgments; a harness result can be mistaken for live integration.
change: Keep the evaluation harness distinct from nova_cortex/witness.py.
Inspect both missed errors and false concerns.
Verify a model switch in the live caller separately from replay results.

glossary.meaning: A package of Nova's body code with a responsibility, such as memory or perception. The name describes software organization, not proof of human-like cognition.
glossary.example: nova_senses groups observation-related code.

glossary.meaning: A Python file, or a package entry point, that defines functions/classes and can import other modules.
glossary.example: model_client.py is one module inside nova_runtime.

glossary.meaning: The learned network and the process of generating output from an input request. It only sees the information actually supplied to that request.
glossary.example: The local llama.cpp process receives Nova's constructed conversation payload.

glossary.meaning: The messages, instructions, observations and retrieved text selected for one model request. Stored information is not automatically present here.
glossary.example: workspace_context builds written background and recall excerpts.

glossary.meaning: A model processes text in token units. Its context window limits the input and output it can handle together, so selection and trimming matter.
glossary.example: Large background files can crowd out recent conversation unless the builder protects it.

glossary.meaning: A numerical representation used to compare related inputs. Similar vectors can retrieve useful candidates; similarity does not prove a remembered claim is true.
glossary.example: The text embedder prepares a query for LanceDB lookup.

glossary.meaning: Storage and search over records with vectors and metadata. The surrounding code decides what to write, search, filter and put into a prompt.
glossary.example: Nova's local archive is reached through hippocampus.py.

glossary.meaning: Find relevant material outside the current request, then add selected results to the model's input. Retrieval and generation are separate operations.
glossary.example: Automatic recall adds a short archive block to chat context.

glossary.meaning: One part receives a function or object from another part and calls it later. This lets the receiver work without hard-coding a particular host.
glossary.example: Chat passes its generation callback into the runtime wake loop.

glossary.meaning: A publisher sends events to interested subscribers. An in-process event bus does not require a network socket.
glossary.example: The runtime publishes activity; the chat interface subscribes and displays it.

glossary.meaning: A producer leaves a unit of work for a consumer to process later. Enqueueing is not the same as successful completion.
glossary.example: The memory indexer processes chat/image entries in a background worker.

glossary.meaning: Processes have separate execution/memory spaces. Threads share their process's memory and need coordination around shared state.
glossary.example: The model server is a separate process; the memory worker is a thread in the host process.

glossary.meaning: HTTP usually exchanges a request and response. WebSocket maintains a connection for messages in both directions. Neither describes an ordinary Python function call.
glossary.example: The chat app serves HTTP and /ws; model inference uses HTTP requests.

glossary.meaning: A smaller set of learned parameters used alongside a base model. Choosing an adapter and ensuring it is loaded by the inference process are different jobs.
glossary.example: KoELS selection and the runtime equip mechanism are separate pieces.

glossary.meaning: Running without the conversation interface. It can use different input/context/output paths, even when it calls the same model.
glossary.example: python -m nova_runtime uses body-owned defaults instead of chat's rich callbacks.

glossary.meaning: A durable record of an attempted or completed operation, including its result. Observability helps reconstruct what actually happened.
glossary.example: A generated claim that a file was read is weaker evidence than a matching action receipt.

glossary.meaning: Nova's software path for checking proposed claims against available evidence. Its own judgments can be wrong and require evaluation.
glossary.example: Live checks are in nova_cortex/witness.py; replay utilities are in nova_witness.

glossary.meaning: Inspecting code without executing it. It can identify many imports and calls but cannot prove which branches ran or resolve all dynamic behavior.
glossary.example: The atlas uses Python's AST and records unknown receivers rather than guessing.

glossary.meaning: The project's architectural test: detachable tools and communication interfaces should be removable without removing the body-owned ability to think and act.
glossary.example: A runtime package alone does not prove full headless context or persistence parity.

glossary.meaning: A regression is previously working behavior that breaks after a change. A contract is the agreed input/output and failure behavior between components.
glossary.example: Renaming a callback argument can break an otherwise valid model-dispatch function.

chat.scenario: Imagine you ask Nova to check a file and explain what it contains.

steps.title: 1. The conversation host receives your message
steps.what: The chat path accepts the request and coordinates the active conversation.
steps.why: The body needs a concrete input, session and output destination.

steps.title: 2. Assemble the information the model will see
steps.what: Written background and relevant archive excerpts are selected for the request.
steps.why: A database or file on disk is invisible to the model until code supplies its contents.

steps.title: 3. Dispatch through the registered model client
steps.what: ModelClient forwards the conversation, context and output callbacks to the registered response implementation.
steps.why: The body can use an injected host interface instead of owning a particular chat window.

steps.title: 4. Generate, interpret and continue
steps.what: The response loop requests inference and interprets reasoning, reply text and action requests.
steps.why: A request to check a file must become an actual operation before its contents can ground an answer.

steps.title: 5. Perform the requested operation
steps.what: When an action is requested, the dispatcher invokes the relevant capability and returns its result.
steps.why: A proposed action is not a performed action. The result needs to reach the next reasoning step.

steps.title: 6. Check relevant claims against evidence
steps.what: The witness path builds checks from available observations and receipts; the response loop handles its verdict.
steps.why: Plausible prose is not proof. The checker itself also needs evidence and evaluation.

steps.title: 7. Deliver and persist the reply
steps.what: The host receives the final callbacks and handles the conversation-facing output and persistence paths.
steps.why: The human needs the result, and later turns need a reliable record of what was delivered.

wake.scenario: Imagine no new message arrives, and the body reaches its next wake cycle.

steps.title: 1. Wake and collect the situation
steps.what: The runtime checks coordination and gathers perception for the wake.
steps.why: Autonomy needs a real trigger and current context, not just a prompt saying to be autonomous.

steps.title: 2. Reflect, then decide
steps.what: Executive code prepares the prompts and interprets the decision path.
steps.why: Reflection is a different phase from deciding whether to act, wait or rest.

steps.title: 3. Consult or update the task board
steps.what: Structured task state records priorities, progress and status.
steps.why: Durable task ids prevent every wake from starting as an unrelated conversation.

steps.title: 4. Execute only the applicable branch
steps.what: The runtime coordinates the next action-capable generation when the relevant conditions hold.
steps.why: A loop that only reflects can produce intentions indefinitely without doing the work.

steps.title: 5. Observe the hosted outcome
steps.what: In chat-hosted mode, callbacks and events connect the wake to output and host coordination. Headless mode uses another path.
steps.why: Shared body code does not guarantee equivalent context or persistence in every host.

memory.scenario: Follow a conversation fragment into storage, then follow a later recall request back out.

steps.title: 1. Queue material for later indexing
steps.what: The host submits chat or image material to the memory ingestion path.
steps.why: Saving a conversation and making it searchable are related but separate operations.

steps.title: 2. Process it in the background
steps.what: A worker consumes queued records and passes them to the store.
steps.why: Embedding and storage can take time; a queue separates the producer from that work.

steps.title: 3. Compute the representation
steps.what: The selected text or image embedding model converts input into a vector.
steps.why: The index compares vectors; it cannot search semantically without a compatible representation.

steps.title: 4. Store and retrieve bounded candidates
steps.what: The store manages local tables, search and formatted recall excerpts.
steps.why: The model needs a small relevant selection, not an entire archive. Similarity is only a candidate-ranking signal.

steps.title: 5. Deliberate recall uses a callable action
steps.what: The response loop can request memory_search through the body dispatcher.
steps.why: Some questions require explicit recall beyond automatic context selection.

steps.title: 6. Automatic recall joins the request context
steps.what: The chat context builder can add selected archive text automatically. Written memory files follow a separate read path.
steps.why: The last mile is injection into the request. Successful storage alone does not establish usable memory.

evidence.scenario: Nova drafts a factual claim. Follow how a check can ask for evidence before delivery.

steps.title: 1. A draft reaches a check boundary
steps.what: The response loop decides whether the current draft needs checking.
steps.why: Checks need a concrete draft and the evidence available for that turn.

steps.title: 2. Build an evidence-limited question
steps.what: The witness receives relevant wire records, receipts and prior checks.
steps.why: An auditor can also invent or overrule incorrectly if its evidence is incomplete.

steps.title: 3. Perform permitted verification reads
steps.what: Where requested and allowed, verification operations obtain additional evidence.
steps.why: A menu that only permits PASS or CONCERN can prevent the model from choosing to read.

steps.title: 4. Keep a durable receipt
steps.what: Receipt helpers retain what an action actually returned.
steps.why: Later diagnosis needs more than a transient UI message saying an action occurred.

steps.title: 5. Revise, accept or use the applicable escalation path
steps.what: The loop interprets the verdict, limits repeated rounds and can invoke an optional deferred second opinion.
steps.why: More checking is not automatically better; latency, false concerns and deadlocks also matter.

computer.scenario: Compare two paths: observing the host and operating the separate computer environment.

steps.title: 1. Identify the host capture path
steps.what: The host vision path begins with the relevant capture/observation code.
steps.why: A screenshot must have a known source before an answer about the screen is meaningful.

steps.title: 2. Interpret captured visual input
steps.what: Vision code sends the appropriate image request to the local multimodal model path.
steps.why: Interpreting an image does not itself supply mouse or keyboard control.

steps.title: 3. Separately, select an execution environment
steps.what: The computer faculty probes available execution backends.
steps.why: Availability differs across machines; a stable interface needs an honest unavailable case.

steps.title: 4. Hands uses the computer shell and X display
steps.what: GUI primitives invoke screenshot/input commands in the selected environment.
steps.why: The display being controlled must match the display being observed. noVNC is a viewer, not the Hands API.

steps.title: 5. Establish the missing end-to-end link
steps.what: The current map has not established an ordinary chat/router caller into this computer faculty.
steps.why: Standalone capability and integrated embodiment are different claims. Trace the full caller and result path before building on it.

koels.scenario: Imagine Nova wants a specialist adapter for a task. Follow choice, equip and process control.

steps.title: 1. Choose the desired working set
steps.what: Selection code uses specialist information to determine a loadout.
steps.why: The reasoning about which specialist is useful is distinct from the mechanics of loading it.

steps.title: 2. Translate the choice into an equip operation
steps.what: The equip mechanism reconciles the requested loadout with the inference setup.
steps.why: An adapter name is not proof that its weights are actually active in the running model.

steps.title: 3. Coordinate model lifecycle when required
steps.what: Model control owns relevant status and restart operations.
steps.why: Changing the loaded working set can affect ongoing generation and must be coordinated.

steps.title: 4. Verify the selected assets and resulting state
steps.what: Manifests describe the available specialists; model assets remain outside this map.
steps.why: A successful design or selection needs a separate check of the actual loaded adapter and inference behavior.
